articles.title: Da esquerda à direita, candidatos ao Senado por SP cobram investigação sobre relações de Vorcaro | G1
articles.standfirst: Enquanto candidatas governistas pedem apuração rigorosa e questionam possíveis tratamentos desiguais em investigações ligadas ao Banco Master, candidatos bolsonaristas defendem o impeachment do ministro do STF Alexandre de Moraes e cobram ação de Davi Alcolumbre.
articles.summary: Enquanto candidatas governistas pedem apuração rigorosa e questionam possíveis tratamentos desiguais em investigações ligadas ao Banco Master, candidatos bolsonaristas defendem o impeachment do ministro do STF Alexandre de Moraes e cobram ação de Davi Alcolumbre.
articles.body:
Os candidatos ao Senado por São Paulo: Simone Tebet (MDB), Marina Silva (Rede), Ricardo Salles (Novo), André do Prado (PL) e Guilherme Derrite (PP). — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo

As revelações sobre uma suposta relação do ministro do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) Alexandre de Moraes com o banqueiro Daniel Vorcaro provocaram reação entre os principais candidatos ao Senado por São Paulo . Da esquerda à direita, os postulantes se manifestaram publicamente defendendo o aprofundamento das investigações sobre o caso, mas com divergências quanto às consequências institucionais imediatas.

Enquanto as candidatas Marina Silva ( Rede ) e Simone Tebet ( PSB ), apoiadas pelo presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT), cobraram transparência nas apurações e ao mesmo tempo criticaram o sigilo sobre outras investigações envolvendo o Banco Master, os candidatos Guilherme Derrite ( PP ), André do Prado ( PL ) e Ricardo Salles ( Novo ), ligados à direita e ao bolsonarismo, adotaram tom mais incisivo em defesa do impeachment de Moraes e vocalizaram críticas diretas ao presidente do Senado, Davi Alcolumbre (União Brasil), a quem atribuem a responsabilidade por não avançar com processos contra ministros do STF.

Ex-ministra do Meio Ambiente, Marina Silva classificou as revelações como "gravíssimas" e defendeu que Moraes seja afastado do cargo para preservar a credibilidade da Corte durante as investigações.

"O ministro Alexandre de Moraes precisa se explicar com toda a transparência que a gravidade dos fatos exige. Mas esse não é o único lado dessa história, precisamos também impedir que esse episódio seja instrumentalizado eleitoralmente ou usado por aqueles que querem deslegitimar o Supremo Tribunal Federal e atacar as nossas instituições", disse a candidata em vídeo publicado nas redes sociais.

Marina também criticou a condução do inquérito sobre o Banco Master pelo ministro André Mendonça. "A lei tem que valer para todos. O caso do filme sobre Jair Bolsonaro, envolvendo Daniel Vorcaro e Flávio Bolsonaro, continua sob sigilo. Por que o ministro Mendonça não adotou ali o mesmo critério?", questionou a candidata, fazendo referência à gravação em que Flávio pede dinheiro ao banqueiro para financiar o filme sobre o pai (ao menos R$ 61 milhões foram repassados à produção).

André Mendonça e Alexandre de Moraes durante sessão plenária do STF — Foto: Antonio Augusto/STF

Simone Tebet (PSB), por sua vez, disse estar "perplexa" e "indignada" com as denúncias. A candidata afirmou que o caso precisa ser apurado com "transparência absoluta em nome do combate à corrupção" e defendeu que o plenário do STF autorize a abertura de um inquérito para investigar Moraes. Segundo ela, a medida permitiria ao ministro exercer seu direito de defesa e, ao mesmo tempo, dar respostas à sociedade sobre as suspeitas reveladas.

Tebet também afirmou que é necessário esclarecer o envolvimento de outras autoridades com o Master e disse que o STF não pode ter "dois pesos e duas medidas" ao tornar públicas informações sobre o caso.

"Nós estamos falando do maior esquema de corrupção do sistema financeiro da história do Brasil. Nós precisamos saber quem mais está envolvido em nome da estabilidade política. Nós estamos falando de possível envolvimento de deputados federais, de senadores, de autoridades de todos os poderes e nós estamos falando também de vídeo e de áudio confessado e confirmado por um candidato à Presidência da República, Flávio Bolsonaro. A lei, ela deve ser aplicada a qualquer pessoa, doa a quem doer", disse Tebet.

Entre os candidatos à direita, as revelações serviram para impulsionar discursos sobre o impeachment de ministros do STF, uma das principais bandeiras do bolsonarismo nas eleições desse ano.

O presidente da Assembleia Legislativa de São Paulo e candidato ao Senado pelo PL, André do Prado, afirmou que Moraes "não tem mais condições de permanecer na cadeira" e defendeu a abertura de processo de impeachment pelo Senado. Segundo ele, as mensagens extraídas do celular de Vorcaro indicam relações incompatíveis com padrões republicanos entre o banqueiro e o ministro do STF, além do procurador-geral da República, Paulo Gonet, e o diretor-geral da Polícia Federal, Andrei Rodrigues.

"Eu não vou ser covarde, eu vou estar sim ao lado dos demais senadores da República que serão eleitos pela direita e se assim for necessário votar impeachment sim de ministro do STF. Sabem por que? Porque ninguém está acima da lei", disse Prado em discurso publicado em suas redes sociais com a legenda "meu posicionamento é claro".

Daniel Vorcaro pergunta se deve ir embora na segunda-feira. — Foto: Reprodução

Em posição semelhante, o ex-secretário estadual de Segurança Pública Guilherme Derrite (PP) publicou vídeo em que declara ser favorável ao impeachment de ministros do Supremo e, sem citar Moraes, diz que esse é um dos anseios da população. "A maioria dos brasileiros de bem não aguentam mais ver os abusos, os absurdos sendo cometidos pelo STF e ninguém faz nada", disse o candidato em trecho de discurso publicado nas redes sociais.

"Antes da gente falar do impeachment – que é necessário, que é fundamental, acho que mais necessário do que nunca – nós precisamos eleger a maioria dos senadores de direita no Brasil. O que adianta ter 119 pedidos se você tem um presidente do Senado Federal que não tem estatura moral para apresentar e para pôr para votação o impeachment?", completou Derrite na publicação.

Já o candidato do Novo, Ricardo Salles, disse que "a situação ficou insustentável" e cobrou diretamente o presidente do Senado, Davi Alcolumbre (União Brasil), que segundo ele estaria se omitindo diante das denúncias.

"A única pessoa no Brasil hoje que pode fazer alguma coisa chama-se Davi Alcolumbre. (...) É ele quem pode dar andamento às dezenas de pedidos de abertura de investigação por crime de responsabilidade", afirmou em vídeo publicano nas redes sociais.

O candidato também aproveitou o episódio para atacar adversários da direita, especialmente André do Prado, a quem acusou de fazer um "teatro" ao defender o impeachment de Moraes.

articles.title: Zema defende prisão de Alexandre de Moraes após caso Banco Master | G1
articles.standfirst: Candidato à Presidência disse que “fruta podre já teria sido expelida” em “qualquer país sério” durante entrevista exibida nesta sexta-feira (4).
articles.summary: O candidato Romeu Zema defende a prisão de Alexandre de Moraes após revelações sobre o Banco Master, afirmando que o ministro seria expelido em um país sério.
articles.body:
Romeu Zema se reúne com empresários do grupo varejista em SP. — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo

O candidato à Presidência pelo Novo, Romeu Zema, defendeu a prisão do ministro do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) Alexandre de Moraes em entrevista ao Estadão nesta sexta-feira (4).

“Por que tem gente aí que fica acima da lei, como esses intocáveis lá do Supremo? É motivo de prisão, não é motivo só de impeachment, não. Um contrato de R$ 129 milhões”, disse, em referência a relatório da Polícia Federal que cita contrato de Viviane Barci de Moraes, esposa do ministro, com Daniel Vorcaro, fundador do Banco Master.

O candidato ainda declarou que, em qualquer país sério, “essa fruta podre já teria sido expelida” há muito tempo. O ex-governador de Minas Gerais afirmou que o Supremo virou “motivo de vergonha nacional”.

Zema entrou no assunto depois de ser questionado sobre como avaliava o envolvimento de figuras de diversos partidos com o banqueiro, como o deputado federal Nikolas Ferreira (PL-MG).

“O brasileiro que acorda cedo, que rala, que paga impostos - que é o que eu fiz a vida toda, por isso essa minha indignação -, quer apuração total, doa a quem doer. Se o Nikolas fez algo errado, que pague. Se o Flávio fez algo errado, que pague também. Lei existe para quê? Agora ser político está acima da lei?”, respondeu.

A declaração do candidato se dá após o surgimento de uma crise no STF. Na terça, o ministro André Mendonça retirou o sigilo de um relatório da Polícia Federal que expõe mensagens e contatos entre o banqueiro Daniel Vorcaro e o ministro Alexandre de Moraes. Moraes, Andrei Rodrigues, diretor-geral da PF, e Paulo Gonet, procurador-geral da República, foram citados por Daniel Vorcaro em mensagens obtidas pela Polícia Federal no celular do dono do Banco Master.

O ministro Alexandre de Moraes, por sua vez, encaminhou na noite de quinta-feira (3) ao presidente da Corte, ministro Edson Fachin, um pedido de investigação contra Mendonça. Na petição, Moraes disse que há presença de fortes indícios da prática de improbidade administrativa, abuso de autoridade, crime de responsabilidade e favorecimento a determinados grupos políticos no exercício da relatoria dos casos Master e INSS.

Fachin deu 5 dias para cada uma das partes se manifestar por escrito. Também passou alguns recados durante participação em um evento do Planalto nesta sexta-feira: disse que os fatos "graves" da "crise Master" que atinge o STF estão em apuração e que nenhuma autoridade está acima da Constituição Federal.

Ainda durante a sabatina, o ex-governador de Minas Gerais também fez uma crítica ao PL, sigla do senador e presidenciável Flávio Bolsonaro. Ao falar sobre as diferenças entre seu partido e o do adversário, já que tinham várias propostas similares, disse: “no Novo, só tem gente ficha limpa; no PL, não”.

Ainda tratando das diferenças que têm em relação a Flávio, destacou sua experiência como “gestor” e o fato de “não ter o rabo preso com nada”. Para o candidato, o país precisa “muito mais de alguém que melhore o setor público” do que “alguém que fica fazendo política como sempre foi feito”.

“Se a política tradicional resolvesse os problemas do Brasil, nós já teríamos resolvido há muito tempo, porque essa turma, PL, PT, PSDB, está aí há quanto tempo liderando o Brasil? Há 30, há 40 anos. E o Brasil ficando cada vez mais para trás”, acrescentou Zema.

O candidato ainda falou sobre algumas de suas propostas, como a redução do número de ministérios de 37 para 22. Ele sugere começar juntando o Ministério da Agricultura, Ministério do Desenvolvimento Agrário e o Ministério da Pesca.

Outro assunto abordado por Zema foi a tributação. Segundo o ex-governador de Minas Gerais, o Brasil tem a “maior tributação disparado no mundo todo, entre países que têm o mesmo nível de desenvolvimento”. Como solução, ele defende “impostos mais inteligentes” e um Estado reduzido.

Para o candidato, “quem ganha muito precisa pagar mais”. Ele se declarou favorável a uma tributação de renda progressiva. “Você tributar quem produz, quem gera riqueza, talvez você esteja matando a galinha dos ovos de ouro. Então, eu acho que tem que ter muito cuidado. A renda tem que ser tributada, sim, fica muito claro. Se tem um salário de R$ 100 mil e o outro tem um salário de R$ 3 mil, quem tem R$ 100 mil de renda precisa pagar uma alíquota maior, não só mais impostos”, disse.

articles.title: Trump administration moves to fast-track oil drilling approvals in Alaska
articles.summary: The Trump administration announced Friday it was proposing to fast-track approvals for oil drilling projects in Alaska after a request from a trade group to do so. The Bureau of Land Management (BLM) issued a proposal that would seek to quickly approve oil and gas drilling in the National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska (NPRA). In…
articles.body:
The Trump administration announced Friday it was proposing to fast-track approvals for oil drilling projects in Alaska after a request from a trade group to do so.

The Bureau of Land Management (BLM) issued a proposal that would seek to quickly approve oil and gas drilling in the National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska (NPRA).

In 1923, then-President Warren Harding set aside the reserve as an emergency oil supply for the Navy. Since that time, drilling projects have bee n approved there , but environmental advocates have also raised concerns about impacts to wildlife .

In its proposal, the BLM said it would consolidate multiple approval procedures into a single review and set timelines that it hopes will “expedite” project approvals.

It said the agency would have to approve some rights-of-way or drilling permit applications within 60 days.

It said its move came in response to a petition from the Alaska Oil and Gas Association, a trade group representing oil and gas companies operating in the state.

That petition called for a “uniform and efficient process to approve production projects similar to those that have already been approved” in the reserve. The trade group’s request also included the 60-day approval timeline.

“Responsible development shouldn’t be held back by redundant paperwork,” BLM Director Steve Pearce said in a statement.

“This is about working smarter, honoring the Trump administration’s commitment to energy security, and ensuring Alaskans directly benefit from the resources in their backyard,” he added.

Environmentalists warned that the move could damage Arctic ecosystems.

“What we’re seeing here is a concerted attack by the Trump administration to greenlight oil and gas drilling in the Western Arctic while ignoring the harm it will cause to these irreplaceable public lands and also the government’s obligation to protect these lands for wildlife and future generations,” said Earthjustice Attorney Erik Grafe.

“These are large-scale, industrial activities that cause permanent damage to sensitive Arctic ecosystems, nearby communities, and the climate,” Grafe continued. “The administration’s proposal flaunts basic environmental laws meant to protect land, wildlife and people and allow for fully informed decision making.”

articles.summary: Plus: 🗺️ Redistricting battle heats up again {beacon} It’s Friday … and no one deserves a long weekend more than our readers! In today’s issue: How about that jobs report? Bartiromo-Fox split Redistricting battle heats up again Clancy verdict not reached Programming note: Hello! We are Colin Meyn and Steff Danielle Thomas filling…
articles.body:
It’s Friday … and no one deserves a long weekend more than our readers!

Programming note : Hello! We are Colin Meyn and Steff Danielle Thomas filling in for Cate. Please send your tips, comments and story ideas to cmeyn@thehill.com or sthomas@thehill.com .

Also: The team will be taking a break for Labor Day. But we will be back in your inbox on Tuesday!

The Associated Press | Alex Brandon and Nam Y. Huh

Today’s jobs report showed the U.S. economy added 162,000 jobs in August, beating expectations that employers added about 53,000 jobs last month. The unemployment rate held steady at 4.1 percent.

That’s a good sign for the health of the economy, after last month’s report showed a slight drop in jobs in July (that was revised up today to plus 21,000 jobs).

But it doesn’t help President Trump ’s push to keep interest rates down.

Why not? The Federal Reserve has two jobs: keep inflation in check and ensure a stable job market.

The better-than-expected job numbers will focus the Fed “squarely on controlling inflation when they meet next in September,” Bill Adams , chief U.S. economist for Fifth Third Commercial Bank, said in a statement.

Inflation remains around 3.4 percent, well above the Fed’s 2 percent target. Markets are now pricing in about a 60 percent chance of a rate hike later this month, according to CME Group’s FedWatch tool , up from 50 percent on Thursday.

Those are fighting words: So far, Trump has had nothing but praise for new Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh . That could change if Warsh oversees a rate hike weeks before the midterms.

Trump celebrated the jobs numbers in a post on Truth Social Friday, while also threatening a new trade war if rates don’t go down.

“LOWER THE RATE OR I’LL STOP TRADING WITH COUNTRIES WITH WHICH WE HAVE A DEFICIT,” the president wrote.

“The Fed Board, with its great new leader, must get smart – BE PATRIOTS for a change,” he added. “High interest rates put the U.S.A. at a very unfair disadvantage, and I won’t allow that to happen!”

Maria Bartiromo , who may have the world record for on-air reactions to jobs reports, is out at Fox News .

She hasn’t hosted her Fox Business Network show for about a month, and Fox News announced on Thursday she won’t be back.

“We thank Maria for her work over the last 12 1/2 years and wish her all the best on her next chapter,” the company said in a statement.

What happened? Fox offered no explanation, and Bartiromo hasn’t said anything publicly since the news broke. Status reported she betrayed the network by sharing information with the White House. The Hill has not confirmed that reporting.

Bartiromo’s lawyer, Bryan Freedman , Friday saying reports she was fired “are absolutely and unequivocally false.”

Trump said he couldn’t believe the news: “Three different shows, always number one. Maria is a total professional, and a true warrior. Her fans, of which there are many, will not be happy. God bless you, Maria!” he wrote on Truth Social.

The map wars are heating up again — this time with courts throwing some curveballs.

Missouri: Republicans wanted a new map that would offer them another chance at picking up a House seat. Instead, the Missouri Supreme Court ruled Thursday that it’s up to the voters in November.

So for now, the old congressional lines are back — including Missouri Democratic Rep. Emanuel Cleaver ’s Kansas City district. GOP officials in the state have vowed to keep fighting the ruling.

Maryland: Democrats won a separate court fight on Thursday to keep a redistricting measure on the ballot in Maryland on Thursday. If approved, it could pave the way for Democrats in the state to redraw its eight House districts and target the one seat held by the GOP.

The catch: The court said the original ballot language was misleading and ordered it rewritten.

So, two states, two court fights, two wins for Democrats — with plenty more redistricting drama ahead.

With just two months until Election Day, Trump called the state Supreme Court’s ruling a “Dark Day for ‘Justice’ in Missouri.”

In a post on Truth Social , he argued that the decision was unconstitutional and could disrupt the midterms.

The president and national Republicans have consistently pushed GOP-led states to redraw congressional maps ahead of November. The Show-Me State was supposed to be one of their biggest opportunities to pick up an additional seat in the House, as both parties wrestle for control of the lower chamber next year.

The Trump administration is asking the Supreme Court to let the Postal Service move ahead with new rules for mail-in ballots — including updated envelope requirements and voter eligibility lists.

A federal judge temporarily blocked the plan last week after a previous high court ruling temporarily lifted restrictions on an executive order issued by Trump, but the clock is ticking.

North Carolina is expected to start mailing ballots Friday, with Alabama following next week.

After seven days of deliberations, jurors in Lindsay Clancy ’s trial threw in the towel on Friday.

Judge William Sullivan said around 11:30 a.m. EDT he had no choice but to declare a mistrial but gave the defense an hour to file an emergency stay before dismissing the jury.

The jury foreperson told the judge Thursday that one juror wasn’t following his guidance on the burden of proof. Sullivan then met with each person on the panel privately, clarified his instructions and sent them to reconsider their positions.

Clancy attorney Kevin Reddington pressed Sullivan to dismiss the juror, but the judge declined . Reddington on Friday urged the judge to send the jury back for further deliberation.

A quick refresher: Clancy, a former labor and delivery nurse, stands accused of killing her three young children at their Massachusetts home in 2023. She has acknowledged the killings, but her defense says she was experiencing postpartum psychosis and should not be held criminally responsible for the deaths. Prosecutors say otherwise.

The jury had already told the judge several times that it could not reach a verdict — which requires a unanimous decision.

A new trial with a fresh jury will likely be scheduled. When or if a jury eventually reaches a decision, there are two very different paths that will emerge.

If Clancy, who is paralyzed from the waist down and uses a wheelchair after jumping from a window following the killings, is found responsible, she faces a potential life sentence.

If she is found not guilty due to mental illness, she could instead be committed to a psychiatric facility.

articles.title: Fetterman faces Dem revolt as bombshell report fuels push to oust him: 'Disgrace'
articles.summary: Sen. Jon Fetterman's leaked texts reveal he dismissed meetings with Children's Hospital of Philadelphia over Medicaid cuts and skipped a police funeral.
articles.body: After a scathing report that called into question Sen. John Fetterman’s willingness to do the basic duties of a senator, some of his Democratic colleagues in Pennsylvania are eyeing ways to dislodge him from the upper chamber. An explosive report from The Wall Street Journal painted Fetterman as a politician more interested in appearing on Fox News to discuss Israel than meeting with paralyzed veterans from his state, and blowing off a funeral for slain police officers because it would have taken too long. And members of his own delegation are furious. REPUBLICANS SAY THEY'D WELCOME FETTERMAN AS GOP EYES BIGGER SENATE MAJORITY "There is a lot I could say about this report of John Fetterman’s pathetic behavior as a senator," Rep. Chris Deluzio, D-Pa., said on X. "But between the laziness, disrespect, and willingness to carry water for a foreign government, it shows us something we already know: this man has no sense of duty." "He is not up for the high office he was elected to — and we in Pennsylvania will do something about it in 2028," he continued. Behind the scenes, The Wall Street Journal’s report revealed through leaked text messages between Fetterman and his aides that the lawmaker was unwilling to do some of the core functions of the job, like meeting with constituents. "John Fetterman is a disgrace," Rep. Brendan Boyle, D-Pa., said on X. "Our state deserves better than a lazy trust fund baby who is too lazy to do the job." In one instance, Fetterman was told by an aide that representatives of the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia (CHOP) wanted to meet over concerns about Medicaid cuts. Fetterman asked why he had to keep meeting with CHOP, and the aide noted that they were worried about "vaccines and Medicaid cuts." FETTERMAN UNDER FIRE AS GOV SHAPIRO PUSHES WILD CARD SENATOR TO 'GET BACK' TO BEING A DEMOCRAT "Well, I’m not," Fetterman responded. "I’m convinced they just want free trips to D.C." Another instance came when an aide told Fetterman that there would be a dress code at a funeral for three police officers killed in Pennsylvania last year, and that the service was expected to last for three hours. "This may be a nonstarter," Fetterman wrote. Years before his time in the Senate, Fetterman rose to prominence as a progressive who appeared to emulate the formula laid out by Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., who he backed early on in his runs for the White House. When Fetterman won his seat in 2022 against Dr. Mehmet Oz, who now runs the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, Fetterman ran on a platform of universal healthcare, pro-labor policies and higher tax rates on wealthy Americans — key hallmarks of progressive politics. Since ascending to the Senate, however, his voting record has shown a more moderate flair, and questions are swirling over whether he will jump ship and join the GOP. He’s bucked his party on several occasions since taking office, too. DNC VICE CHAIR ATTACKS DEMOCRATIC SEN. JOHN FETTERMAN: 'YOU’RE A MESS' During the government shutdown fight last year, he joined Republicans as Democrats stayed unified in their push to renew lapsing Obamacare tax credits, has become one of the most vocal proponents of Israel, and helped to confirm some of President Donald Trump’s nominees, including Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin — notably, he voted against his old political rival Oz. The desire to boot Fetterman extends beyond just his colleagues in the Pennsylvania congressional delegation. Pennsylvania state Rep. Malcolm Kenyatta, who is the vice chair of the Democratic National Committee, has his sights set on Fetterman, too. articles.title: NC elections officials alter mail ballot rules just before they’re mailed out
articles.summary: The North Carolina State Board of Elections approved new guidelines Friday regarding mail-in ballots, hours before those same ballots were sent to voters. The new guidelines pertain to the standards the board will use to decide whether to count a mail-in ballot — including requiring officials to disqualify a ballot if its signature does not…
articles.body:
The North Carolina State Board of Elections approved new guidelines Friday regarding mail-in ballots, hours before those same ballots were sent to voters.

The new guidelines pertain to the standards the board will use to decide whether to count a mail-in ballot — including requiring officials to disqualify a ballot if its signature does not match the name assigned to the application on the return envelope.

Other changes specify that only a near relative or legal guardian can deliver a voter’s mail-in ballot in person on their behalf, and they require officials to disqualify ballots if more than one is included in a return envelope.

The new guidelines were debated between board officials , with the two Democrats dissenting.

“To my mind, we’re doing an end run around the process that we said we wanted to do,” Democratic member Siobhan Millen said at the board’s meeting. “It may not affect you as you’re filling it out, but it affects whether your ballot counts — that’s huge. So, an effort to say this is just a process thing, I think is incorrect.”

Stacy Eggers, a Republican member of the board, defended the new standards, saying, “This is simply guidance, updated guidance, I might add, as to what the board and staff at the county level will do and how they will process things.”

The guidelines were approved as numbered memos after similar rulings from the board couldn’t go into effect — despite the state’s Rules Review Commission unanimously approving them — due to a provision in state law that delays such rules if 10 or more formal objections are received.

The previous rulings must be decided by the North Carolina Legislature in its next session.

The first batch of ballots was initially promised to be sent out to more than 46,000 voters, even as the ballot’s validity is still being decided at the federal level.

The Justice Department asked the Supreme Court on Thursday to clear the way for the U.S. Postal Service to implement President Trump’s executive order targeting mail voting in time for the midterms.

The service’s plan would mandate that states’ mail-in ballots meet design requirements — such as unique barcodes and an official logo — and require election officials to upload lists of voters who are eligible to vote by mail; otherwise, the Postal Service will refuse to deliver ballots.

In a filing last week , North Carolina Assistant Deputy Attorney General Marc Brunton argued against the service’s rules because of “the very short time available and the untested technology that the Rule relies on.”

He argued that the mail-in ballot system was “particularly important” for parts of western North Carolina in the wake of Hurricane Helene, which hit the region in 2024 and reportedly did $60 billion in damage.

articles.title: ‘Treasonous scum’: Trump attacks media over Iran war coverage
articles.summary: Nobody wants to see the United States fail. Nobody wants American service members put in greater danger. Nobody wants our military unprepared to respond to another threat. But that does not mean Americans have to pretend this war is going according to plan.
articles.body:
President Trump is attacking news organizations reporting on the strain the Iran war has placed on America’s weapons stockpiles, calling those outlets “treasonous” and accusing them of wanting the U.S. to lose because they specifically don’t want to see him win.

He took to Truth Social to vent, writing : “The people and Media Outlets that keep harping on the fact that we have no ammunition (And they are 100% wrong!), are actually treasonous. They do it because they would rather see the United States LOSE a War that we’re easily WINNING, than see me WIN!”

He went on , saying: “For the treasonous SCUM that refuses to accurately report on our Military Operation in Iran, we have virtually unlimited amounts of Mid to High Grade Ammunition, far more than we could ever use for this, or for any other War”

But reporting from multiple outlets paints a very different picture.

The Hill points to an estimate from analysts at the Center for Strategic and International Studies that shows by late July, the U.S. had an estimated 759 to 827 Patriot interceptors remaining — down from roughly 2,330 before the war.

The Washington Post this week reported that senior military officials warned Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth that continuing the current pace of operations could become unsustainable and limit America’s ability to respond to threats elsewhere, even here in America.

And reportedly, some military leaders issued what are known as “non-concurs,” essentially putting their disagreement on the record while still following orders. According to the report, the Navy, in particular, is facing significant strain, with its top admiral reportedly warning that the service cannot sustain the current level of support without an anticipated end date.

The Army’s top civilian leader, Secretary Daniel P. Driscoll, quit this week, handing in his resignation after repeatedly clashing with Hegseth due to his firing or forcing out more than a dozen senior military officers and generals during his tenure.

Many Americans disagreed with the decision to go to war. We were also told this war was not supposed to be open-ended. The administration initially talked about a roughly six-week timeline. We are now in the seventh month.

Nobody wants to see the United States fail. Nobody wants American service members put in greater danger. Nobody wants our military unprepared to respond to another threat. But that does not mean Americans have to pretend this war is going according to plan.

This was a war of choice. The administration bypassed Congress to enter it, and now Americans are being asked to trust the administration’s assessment of progress while questions about weapons, readiness, military deployments and an endgame continue to mount. You can support the troops and still question the mission. If the goal still is actually to bring this conflict to an end, the administration owes the American people more than all caps messages on Truth Social. Provide us with an objective and an exit strategy.

Lindsey Granger is a NewsNation contributor and co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising.” This column is an edited transcription of her on-air commentary.

President Trump signed an executive order Friday afternoon related to the beef industry , according to the White House.

Trump announced last month that the U.S. would pause higher tariffs on ground beef imports for 90 days, allowing up to 300,000 metric tons to enter the country without the higher “out-of-quota” tariff rate.

Trump said the move would help lower costs for consumers while giving the administration time to rebuild the U.S. cattle herd and support ranchers.

The plan has come under heavy criticism from Republicans and ranchers alike .

articles.title: Non-citizen police officers approved after Dem says ICE 'invasion' 'sends a message'
articles.summary: Danbury, Connecticut's city council voted 18-2 to let non-citizen immigrants and DACA recipients serve as police officers amid ongoing ICE raids.
articles.body: After a week of ICE raids, the Democrat-dominated City Council of Danbury, Connecticut, voted nearly unanimously to approve non-citizen legal residents serving as police officers. Under the new guidance, approved in an 18-2 vote, non-citizen legal residents and Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) recipients living in Danbury are allowed to serve as police officers in Danbury. One city council member, Democrat Joe Britton, remarked that the vote "sends a message to our immigrant community at large that you are welcome in Danbury." ICE operations in the area resulted in more than 60 arrests, according to local reports. The arrests prompted public outrage in the community, including from city officials such as Britton, who called the raids "frightening." BORDER CZAR TOM HOMAN FIRES BACK AFTER DEMOCRAT CHRIS MURPHY CLAIMS ICE IS ‘TERRORIZING LITTLE KIDS’ The only two council members to vote against the measure were Republicans, while the council’s 17 Democrats and one Republican voted in favor. Before the vote, Britton said that "what we have here is an opportunity." He noted that "though this definitely wasn’t planned to be on the agenda on the end of a federal invasion of immigration officials in Danbury … I do think it's timely." "There is no reason to vote against this, and if you do vote against this, I truly question your moral compass," he added. Britton emphasized that this change "is legal, it's allowed" and said it has been recommended. Britton told Fox News Digital that "Danbury is an immigrant city, and I believe someone who is lawfully here, committed to our community, and willing to raise their hand and take an oath to protect and serve should have the opportunity to do so." He added that "this change does not lower Danbury’s standards for becoming a police officer. It simply allows otherwise qualified lawful permanent residents and DACA recipients to apply and compete for these positions." He noted that "every applicant must still satisfy the same training, background, character, and certification requirements required of any other officer," saying, "This was about expanding the pool of qualified applicants while maintaining the same high standards our residents expect from their police department." Similarly, Taylor O'Brien, a spokesperson for the Danbury city government, told Fox News Digital that council "amended its ordinance in accordance with Connecticut's Police Officer Standards and Training Council, allowing legal permanent residents and DACA recipients to apply to become officers in the Danbury Police Department." DEM SENATE NOMINEE CHANGES TUNE ON ICE AFTER VOWING NOT 'ONE MORE DIME' FOR AGENCY O'Brien said that "this standard is followed by over 30 municipalities in Connecticut and several states across the country" and that it "opens Danbury's applicant pool to otherwise qualified candidates, including legal Danbury residents, who are currently applying to be police officers in other communities." In 2020, the Connecticut Police Officer Standards and Training Council "partially waived" the citizenship requirement, extending eligibility for law enforcement candidates in Connecticut to lawful permanent residents and DACA recipients, according to the Connecticut Department of Emergency Services and Public Protection. O'Brien added that Danbury Mayor Roberto Alves, a Democrat, "ensures Danbury maintains a rigorous hiring process for our Police Officers," adding that "this amendment should encourage qualified residents from the Danbury community to apply to serve the City they call home." According to the Danbury News Times, Alves himself immigrated to the U.S. as an "undocumented child" and gained citizenship in 2017. The outlet quoted Alves saying he is "glad the City Council approved" the measure. Alves emphasized that "the standards are not being lowered" and that "every applicant still has to meet the same rigorous background, training, fitness and professional standards required of any Danbury police officer." "What we are doing is giving qualified people an opportunity to compete for the job," said Alves. "For a diverse city like Danbury, it strengthens our recruitment pool and gives us another opportunity to hire talented people who understand and care about the community they want to serve." On July 25, 2025, Jamaican national Jon Luke Evans, who was serving as a reserve officer with the Old Orchard Beach, Maine, Police Department, was arrested on charges related to unlawfully attempting to purchase a gun. articles.title: ‘Fiesta Mexicana’: El-Sayed campaign plans festive 9/11 while remembrance is missing from public schedule
articles.summary: Abdul El-Sayed's campaign scheduled county fair and Fiesta Mexicana events on 9/11's 25th anniversary, raising questions about the Michigan Senate race.
articles.body: While Americans prepare to mark the 25th anniversary of 9/11, Abdul El-Sayed’s public campaign schedule for that day makes no mention of a remembrance event, but includes a Mexican festival, a farmers market and a county fair. As of Friday morning, El-Sayed’s campaign website listed staff and volunteers for Grand Rapids’ Fiesta Mexicana, a nearby farmers market and the Allegan County Fair, while El-Sayed himself was scheduled to make a stop on his "Shouldn’t Be This Hard" tour. After Fox News Digital asked about the lack of a 9/11 remembrance on the public schedule, El-Sayed’s campaign said the Democrat nominee "will be attending a 9/11 remembrance memorial event that day," though the event was not listed on his campaign website. FOX NEWS MEDIA ANNOUNCES EXTENSIVE 9/11 ANNIVERSARY COVERAGE FROM GROUND ZERO, PENTAGON AND SHANKSVILLE The events listed on the campaign schedule have a notably more festive tone. Fiesta Mexicana, for instance, describes itself as "three days of mariachi, folklórico and forty-some vendors" that uses "music, food, dance and good company" to "make sure Mexican culture is known, understood and celebrated in West Michigan — on our own terms." El-Sayed’s campaign instructs supporters to "bring some Mexican swag" and "go inside to enjoy the music and get some food." The Allegan County Fair, meanwhile, features live entertainment, food, games and rides. El-Sayed’s campaign pointed out, that of the four events flagged by Fox News Digital — Fiesta Mexicana, the farmers market, the county fair and the candidate’s tour event — the Senate candidate would not be attending two of them, though would not specify which ones. The campaign did not explain why El-Sayed's website did not list the 9/11 remembrance memorial event on his list of upcoming events, but it did underscore in a comment to Fox News Digital that El-Sayed views 9/11 as a horrific moment in history. "The September 11th terrorist attacks were an evil attack on America's freedom and he will be joining Michiganders in remembering the 25th anniversary," El-Sayed’s spokeswoman told Fox News Digital. BIDEN-WORLD VETERAN ISSUES STARK WARNING ABOUT ABDUL EL-SAYED AS HE CROSSES PARTY LINES The Michigan Senate hopeful has a complicated relationship with 9/11. Twitch streamer Hasan Piker, whom El-Sayed had campaigned alongside, caused him a headache early in the campaign when a clip of the streamer saying that America "deserved 9/11" resurfaced. El-Sayed called the statement "dumb," though did not disavow Piker. Later, old blogs and social media posts where El-Sayed made controversial statements about the terrorist attacks began to surface. articles.title: Former Kentucky Gov. Matt Bevin arrested on film set
articles.summary: Former Kentucky Gov. Matt Bevin (R) was arrested Thursday at a movie set over an outstanding warrant in his divorce and child support case. Bevin was booked into a Louisville jail that evening after the Bourbon County Sheriff’s Office arrested Bevin in Paris, Ky., during the filming of a Christmas movie. The former governor was…
articles.body:
Former Kentucky Gov. Matt Bevin (R) was arrested Thursday at a movie set over an outstanding warrant in his divorce and child support case.

Bevin was booked into a Louisville jail that evening after the Bourbon County Sheriff’s Office arrested Bevin in Paris, Ky., during the filming of a Christmas movie.

The former governor was playing a “featured extra” in the film and was talking to the film’s lead actor when deputies arrived, property owner Jessica Mohr told Kentucky Public Radio, which first reported the arrest.

“The sheriff showed up and was asking some people if they’d seen his picture, and a young man was like, ‘I think that gentleman’s inside,’” Mohr said. “And yeah, he was arrested.”

Bourbon County Sheriff Tony Asbury confirmed in a press release that he had an active warrant for Bevin’s arrest and that his office had received a tip that the former governor was involved in a film project at the horse farm estate.

“The Bourbon County Sheriff’s Office contacted Former Governor Bevin at the location reported and he was taken into custody shortly after and lodged into the Bourbon-Nicholas County Region Detention Center without any issues as Bevin was very cooperative,” Asbury said in a statement.

The warrant was issued after Jefferson Family Court Judge Angela Johnson found Bevin in contempt for failing to turn over financial documents in a case involving his ex-wife, Glenna Bevin.

Johnson sentenced him in June to 60 days in jail and a $500 fine. He was issued an earlier warrant for failing to appear for a May court hearing, which he claimed he could not make because a boulder crashed into his home in Maine.

Matt Bevin, who served as governor from 2015 to 2019, lost in his reelection bid to current Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear (D). His running mate at the time, Ralph Alvarado, is currently the Republican candidate in Kentucky’s 6th Congressional District to replace Rep. Andy Barr (R-Ky.), who is running for Senate.

“No one who thought it was a good idea to run alongside Matt Bevin should represent the families of Kentucky’s Sixth Congressional District,” the Kentucky Democratic Party said in a statement.

A spokesperson for Alvarado said Bevin should be held responsible for failing to follow the court’s orders.

“Court orders are not optional, and everyone should comply with the court’s directive,” spokesperson Andrew Westberry told The Hill. “Failure to do so has consequences.”

articles.title: Pennsylvania Democrat blasts Fetterman as ‘lazy trust fund baby’
articles.summary: Rep. Brendan Boyle (D-Pa.) slammed his fellow Pennsylvania Democratic colleague Sen. John Fetterman on Thursday, calling him a “lazy trust fund baby” following reports that Fetterman has been neglecting his duties as a senator. “John Fetterman is a disgrace,” the congressman said in a post on social platform X. “Our state deserves better than a…
articles.body:
Rep. Brendan Boyle (D-Pa.) slammed his fellow Pennsylvania Democratic colleague Sen. John Fetterman on Thursday, calling him a “lazy trust fund baby” following reports that Fetterman has been neglecting his duties as a senator.

“John Fetterman is a disgrace,” the congressman said in a post on social platform X . “Our state deserves better than a lazy trust fund baby who is too lazy to do the job.” Fetterman has said that his parents financially supported him into his 40s.

The statement was sparked by a Wall Street Journal report that alleged the senator avoided meeting with three disabled service members but opted to do an interview with Fox News on Israel and the war in Iran.

He also reportedly attempted to dodge a meeting with the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, which was concerned about Medicaid funding cuts in last year’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act.

At the time, Fetterman received backlash from Boyle for saying that the act’s long voting process caused him to miss an “entire trip to the beach.”

“I will do whatever it takes, stay up for 48 straight hours, 72 straight hours, do whatever it takes to block this bill from becoming law,” Boyle said at the time . “And that should be the attitude, frankly, of every Democratic member of the House and Senate.”

The report noted that for the past year, Fetterman attended 26 of the 31 full hearings for his assigned committees but did not speak in 20 of them, which sparked outrage from other Pennsylvania Democrats.

“There is a lot I could say about this report of John Fetterman’s pathetic behavior as a Senator,” Rep. Chris Deluzio (D-Pa.) said Thursday on X . “But between the laziness, disrespect, and willingness to carry water for a foreign government, it shows us something we already know: this man has no sense of duty.”

“He is not up for the high office he was elected to — and we in Pennsylvania will do something about it in 2028,” he added.

Democratic National Committee Vice Chair and Pennsylvania state Rep. Malcolm Kenyatta (D) told NewsNation on Sunday that Fetterman “is somebody who has spent the past few years not doing his job. He is a part-time senator, full-time commentator on Fox News.”

In a separate Friday statement , Kenyatta said that “2028 can’t come soon enough” and that Fetterman “barely showed up as LG and is constantly MIA as our Senator.”

articles.title: France 'will reject extremism' and Le Pen in presidential election, Haddad says
articles.summary: Polls suggest far-right veteran Marine Le Pen is on course to become France’s next president, though the race remains in its early stages. But EU minister Ha...
articles.body:
French minister for European Affairs, Benjamin Haddad, told Euronews he's "quite confident" the French electorate will reject extremism, and won't elect a far-right candidate to replace President Emmanuel Macron in next year's election.

His comments come days after an Elabe poll for BFMTV/La Tribune Dimanche showed Le Pen dwarfing all other candidates; predicting her to win between 34% and 35.5% of first-round votes.

Le Pen, the president of the far-right National Rally party, was cleared to stand in July despite an appeals court upholding an embezzlement conviction against her.

"We still have a long way to go before the election, but I'm quite confident that the French, like they've done so many, many times, will refuse extremism," Haddad said on Euronews' interview programme 12 Minutes With .

"The French people have repeatedly said no to extremism, to euroscepticism, and populism," he said.

He said next spring's 2027 election will be "a tough one, like every election," but added that he "never trusts the polls," arguing that they have been wrong in the past.

"When I personally started supporting Emmanuel Macron in 2016, he was far, far behind in the polls," said Haddad, who belongs to the same political party as Macron, Renaissance (formerly La République En Marche!).

Ahead of the 2017 elections, Macron rose from third position in the polls after he declared his candidacy in November 2016, to briefly polling ahead of Le Pen weeks ahead of the elections.

He gained 24% of the vote in the first round in April 2017, then won the presidency in the second round with 66% of the vote, in contrast with Le Pen's 34%. This margin narrowed significantly in the second round of the 2022 elections, when Macron beat Le Pen with 59% of the vote to her 41%.

Haddad said the French are "deeply European" and will ultimately reject Le Pen.

"The French are proud of the role that their country is playing on the European stage," he said.

"Marine Le Pen, for a long time, has been the candidate of 'Frexit'," he said, referring to the demand by some on the fringes of French politics, who called for France to leave the EU and the eurozone.

The prospect of France leaving the EU was a strong component in Le Pen's 2012 and 2017 manifestos. At present, she still maintains a staunchly eurosceptic stance, pledging to cut back on Europe's contributions to the bloc and calling for the scrapping of norms, but no longer explicitly advocates for a referendum on France's membership of the EU.

"She's been the candidate [standing for] leaving the eurozone. She was the candidate of the alliance with Vladimir Putin," Haddad said.

"She's trying to make people forget about all of this and sometimes even says that it never happened, even though we know her stance on the European Union for a long time."

Despite his conviction that the French public will vote against Le Pen, Haddad warned politicians from other parties should approach the rise of the far-right and populism "with a lot of humility."

"Our first responsibility is to continue to deliver on results. All the issues that we're discussing, from migration and security, from competitiveness, prosperity, from defending the security of Europeans against foreign threats, we have to continue to deliver on this, Haddad explained.

He went on to say that continuing to "campaign, to meet the French, to listen to voters, and to respond" is also central in this mission.

The linchpin to his proposal to beat the far-right will perhaps be the most challenging of all to attain, given the fragmented nature of the race with eight months to go until the first round of elections.

"We need to unify around a candidate, because right now we have a lot of talent in the centre, but we have a fragmented political offer," Haddad said.

Around 30 figures have already expressed their ambition to run. Two of those considered likely candidates are Macron's former prime ministers: centrist Gabriel Attal (Renaissance) and centre-right figure Édouard Philippe (Horizons), while conservative candidate Bruno Retailleau (Les Républicains) is one of the President's former Ministers.

On the hard-left, Jean-Luc Mélenchon (La France Insoumise) is vying to be President, while other candidates running on the left include Marine Tondelier (the Greens) and MEP Raphaël Glucksmann (Place Publique).

"I think by the end of the year we will have one candidate that can rally the centre and the centre-right and then we will make a case." Some candidates have suggested they would consider partaking in a primary.

Extremism 'not the answer to uncertainties'

Still, Le Pen remains the front-runner in the polls. In 2024, her party won the European Parliamentary elections in France with more than twice the number of votes of Macron's party, pushing the president to call a snap election at the time.

Haddad conceded that global uncertainties fuel populism's popularity, pointing to the fact that many of the certainties people had before "are crumbling."

"Trade is being weaponised as a tool of pressure. You see China's subsidised overcapacities coming to our markets and destabilising our industries. Our traditional alliances are being questioned; there's the war of Russian aggression on our continent," he explained.

"When you have these uncertainties, and the pillars on which we built our European Union and our transatlantic alliance are questioned, this very often paves the way for radical answers," Haddad added, noting that he doesn't believe those answers are right

"I don't think that in a world where you have the pressure from China, from the US, the threat coming from Russia, we would be stronger going it alone. I don't think we'd be stronger looking inwards."

The first round of the French presidential election will take place on 18 April 2027, while the second will be held on 2 May 2027 if no candidate wins a majority of votes.

images.caption: France 'will reject extremism' and Le Pen in presidential election, Haddad says

Four House Democrats are headed to Dallas next week as the Republican National Committee holds a first-of-its-kind midterm convention, House leadership announced Friday.

Democratic Reps. Robert Garcia (Calif.), Jason Crow (Colo.), Madeleine Dean (Pa.) and Sydney Kamlager-Dove (Calif.) make up the delegation, which will partner with local leaders and the Texas Democratic Party on the ground.

“While swing seat House Republicans try to hide from their record of raising costs on working families, gutting Medicaid to fund tax breaks for billionaire donors and supporting a reckless war of choice in Iran, House Democrats will be present to hold them accountable,” House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) said in a release.

Jeffries accused MAGA extremists of “partying with their super rich donors in Dallas” as Americans feel the sting of high prices.

“Americans are being crushed by rising costs. Republicans don’t care—they’re in Dallas, celebrating an out of touch President whose tariffs and wars are making things worse. We’re going to hold them accountable,” Crow said on the social platform X.

The Democrats’ Texas visit acts as counterprogramming to the RNC’s convention, which is aimed at highlighting Republican candidates and energizing the party’s voters ahead of the high-stakes midterm election. Vice President Vance is giving a speech on the first night, and President Trump is set to deliver the closing-night keynote address.

The Dallas-based event comes as Republicans fight to hold on to the Texas Senate seat up for grabs in November and as both parties battle over a handful of highly competitive House seats after GOP-friendly redistricting reshaped the state’s congressional maps last year.

articles.body:
Rep. Suhas Subramanyam (D-Va.) said Thursday that the FBI and Justice Department (DOJ) informed him they had wiretapped his past phone conversations with a Virginia state lawmaker.

Subramanyam’s office shared photos of two letters he said he received from the agencies, dated from July and August, notifying him they monitored some of his calls with Virginia state Senate President Pro Tempore Louise Lucas (D).

The representative slammed this action as “deeply concerning” in his Thursday statement , accusing the Trump administration of trying to intimidate Democrats.

A federal judge authorized the phone call interception in April, according to the letters. A month later, federal agents conducted a search of Lucas’ office and a cannabis dispensary she co-owned as part of this investigation. The state legislator has denied any wrongdoing and claimed the federal probe was politically motivated.

Subramanyam’s statement described called the timing of the phone tapping and investigation into the Virginia state senate leader “extremely suspicious.”

He noted the probe occurred within the same period Virginia Democrats were pushing for a redistricting referendum — an effort that Lucas championed.

The Virginia representative also pointed to his role on the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform as a potential reason for the agencies’ scrutiny, noting he and other Democrats were demanding answers from the DOJ at the time over its handling of the investigation into late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

“This should concern anyone who believes in a real Department of Justice that serves the American people and not a singular president,” Subramanyam said.

“If this surveillance was done to scare us and to get Democrats to stop pushing back against [President] Trump’s political overreach, they are mistaken,” he continued. “We will not back down. We will continue our investigations into this President and his corrupt administration.”

The Hill has reached out to the DOJ and Lucas for comment. The FBI declined to comment.

articles.title: Supreme Court backs Republicans in election ad rate dispute
articles.summary: Republicans asked the high court to allow party committees to receive the same ad discounts that candidates themselves benefit from.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court on Friday handed a win to Republicans by ensuring that party committees paying for TV advertisements in the upcoming midterm elections can take advantage of the same discounts that candidates get. The justices blocked a ruling by the Richmond, Virginia-based 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals that had invalidated a recently announced Federal Communications Commission policy. Only one member of the court, liberal Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, objected to the majority’s decision. The decision means that the often sharply discounted rates will apply to committees and candidates alike as litigation continues. The National Republican Congressional Committee and the National Republican Senatorial Committee, with the backing of the Trump administration, had asked the Supreme Court to block the appeals court ruling. In the unsigned order, the court said that the committees had shown they were likely to suffer “irreparable harm” if the appeals court ruling was not blocked because broadcasters have already started declining to offer them the discounted rates for ads. Taken together with a Supreme Court ruling in June that lifted previous restrictions on committee expenditures, the latest decision represents a significant boon for Republicans. In the June ruling, the Supreme Court struck down federal limits on “coordinated party communications,” caps that used to govern how much national party organizations like the Democratic and Republican Senate campaign committees could spend directly in concert with their candidates. The two rulings allow Republicans to stretch their party committee dollars even further by allowing them to spend more committee money at lower rates. Democrats will have the same power, but the decision is of less help to them because their candidates are already, on the whole, better funded, and the Democratic National Committee has more than $100 million less in its coffers than the Republican National Committee does. Several Democratic House and Senate candidates, including Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., challenged the March public notice issued by the FCC. In an Aug. 25 ruling, the appeals court ruled that the party committees are not entitled to the same discounts as candidates. Democratic candidates have generally raised significantly more money than their rivals for years, but Republican committees have far more money banked away for the fall, so the ruling allows the cash-flush GOP committees to help narrow that gap.

images.caption: The Supreme Court is seen through the viewfinder of a television camera.

articles.title: Supreme Court sides with GOP in fight over TV ad rates; Jackson dissents
articles.summary: The Supreme Court on Friday lifted a ruling that prevented party committees from accessing cheaper advertising rates in the lead-up to November’s elections, siding with Republicans, for now, in an emergency case that drew staunch Democratic opposition. articles.body:
The Supreme Court on Friday lifted a ruling that prevented party committees from accessing cheaper advertising rates in the lead-up to November’s elections, siding with Republicans, for now, in an emergency case that drew staunch Democratic opposition.

Federal law mandates that broadcast stations offer their lowest available rate in the 60 days preceding a general election. Everyone agrees candidates get the discount, but whether political parties and joint fundraising committees can, too, has come under question.

The court appeared to split 8-1, though the justices don’t have to disclose their votes in emergency decisions publicly. The majority said that federal courts had no authority yet to intervene in the dispute.

Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, the court’s junior liberal justice, publicly dissented. In a one-paragraph opinion, she explained the lower panel likely had authority to move ahead.

Republicans’ Senate and House campaign arms — boasting a cash advantage and backed by the Trump administration — brought the fight to the Supreme Court after Democratic candidates sued to stop them from accessing the cheaper rate.

The Supreme Court majority on Friday said the challengers couldn’t come to the federal judiciary yet because their review petition with the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) was still pending. The majority went on to agree that party committees would suffer irreparable harm if they didn’t intervene.

“Current and future recissions will require the party committees to pay more for advertising space, thereby hampering their efforts to reach the electorate in the critical weeks leading up to the midterms,” the court’s unsigned opinion reads.

Democrats won before the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit. In a 2-1 decision, the panel ruled the FCC’s notice asserting the committees could enjoy the discount wasn’t legal.

In their Supreme Court filings, Republicans largely centered their case on the notion that the judges had no authority to get involved, describing the notice as a “staff-level guidance document.”

National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC) Communications Director Joanna Rodriguez reacted to the ruling by calling the lawsuit “frivolous and partisan.”

“The NRSC structured itself and our campaigns to maximize the fall of coordinated spending limits and achieve unprecedented cost-sharing on polling, research, critical infrastructure, advertising, and direct mail,” Rodriguez said in a statement. “Today’s decision ensures those efforts will be even further strengthened as the candidate rate on our coordinated television spending stretches our hard dollars further than ever before.”

Republicans’ emergency appeal garnered support from the Trump administration, which similarly told the high court the lower courts had no authority.

“The challengers claim, and the court of appeals agreed, that the notice injures them by making it cheaper for their opponents to run campaign advertisements,” Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote to the justices. “But the notice does not grant favored treatment to one side or the other; instead, the notice’s interpretation offers the same benefit to all sides”

Democrats insisted to the justices the lower courts acted properly and had power to intervene.

“On both reviewability and the merits, Applicants and the United States want to talk about everything except the text of the directly pertinent statutes. That is because on both questions, the text directly supports Candidates,” they wrote in court filings.
